paper_title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Most questions asked of an organizations data are routine: how many orders shipped last month, which customers lapsed, what region earned. On 1 BIRD (Li et al., 2023b), benchmark of large real databases with noisy values, many high-scoring systems write SQL token by token and sample several queries per question before voting, reranking or revising (Pourreza et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026), and LLM agents that explore the database with tools are among the most accurate. Run as such an agent, Claude Opus 5.5 answered 77.26% of 796 questions on held-out BIRD training databases correctly in our runs, at about 2 cents per question at list price. For an organization asking ten thousand questions day that is about $200 day, over $70,000 year, with every question sent to hosted model, even though BIRD hands the agent an expert-written hint per question that real users do not. Yet of the 311 questions it answered correctly in 400-question sample, our one-pass 7B model alone also got 228 right. Kahnemans split between fast, automatic System 1 and slow, deliberate System 2 (Kahneman, 2011) fits this situation, as do model cascades that send easy inputs to cheap model (Chen et al., 2024), and our design was inspired by TypeSafes Jev, System One model that returns typed decisions instead of free text (Almeida, 2026). Our System 1 is one-pass, non-autoregressive 7B model that runs on hardware the organization already owns, where each question it answers costs only electricity and never leaves that machine; System 2, the agent, is called only when System 1 is unsure. We ask how much of the agents bill one local model can remove without costing accuracy, whether such model is tied to the SQL engine it was trained on, and how far an agents accuracy on public benchmarks can be trusted when the agent may have seen them. LuthorSQL goes back to slot filling (Xu et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018a). LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022) on OmniSQL-7B (Li et al., 2025) reads the schema and question once and fills every slot of bounded plan grammar in parallel; deterministic Evidence: movie Batman refers to title = Batman; tallest refers to max(height_inches) Question: Among the actors who starred in the movie Batman , which one of them is the tallest ? movie MovieID Title Rating . . . characters MovieID ActorID . . . actor ActorID Name Date of Birth Height (Inches) . . . schema, encoded once per database Plan (one forward pass): projection agg = none, actor.Name filter movie.Title = Batman order actor."Height (Inches)" DESC limit 1 distinct no group by none require characters compiler Compiled SQL: SELECT T1.Name FROM actor AS T1 JOIN characters AS T2 ON T1.ActorID = T2.ActorID JOIN movie AS T3 ON T2.MovieID = T3.MovieID WHERE T3.Title = Batman ORDER BY T1."Height (Inches)" DESC LIMIT 1 column chosen by slot (word links drawn for illustration) stored value (pointed at, never written) foreign key (known) join built by the compiler (the plan lists characters only in its require slot) schema + question: one pass, slot heads up to 32 distinct plans (21 for this question) compile (Steiner tree over FKs) execute (read-only) validator scores each candidate pick: best live candidate Figure 1: How LuthorSQL answers question. The slot heads, read after the question, point to schema columns and to stored value; the word links are drawn for illustration, since the model scores slot states, not word alignments. No question word names characters; the plan lists it only in its require slot, and the compiler builds the join along the foreign-key path between movie and actor. The same pass yields up to 32 distinct plans (21 for this question), found by best-first search, which are compiled, executed and scored by the validator. Example: BIRD train question 740 (movie, held-out database), answered correctly. compiler turns each plan into SQL, taking joins from the foreign-key graph; and second adapter scores the executed candidates and picks one (Figure 1). The grammar covers 84.6% of BIRD dev gold queries, one reason to pair System 1 with an agent. Both adapters sit on the same frozen backbone weights, which can be loaded once, so LuthorSQL is one 7B model with two small adapters, not an ensemble of LLMs; LuthorSQL means this two-adapter system throughout (singleadapter variant: Appendix C; path to this design and failed attempts: Appendices and B). Contributions. LuthorSQL, one-pass slot-filling System 1 on 7B backbone with typed plan grammar, lazy k-best candidates and validator trained on hard negatives: 68.03% on BIRDs hidden test set at 0.84 per question on one GPU, the same accuracy with 8-bit weights in about 9 GB, and, translated without retraining, 57.159.3% on Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL and DuckDB against 60.17% in SQLite on BIRD dev. confidence cascade with an LLM agent, tested in registered experiments on data that 2 played no part in choosing it. Calling Opus 5.5 only below validator margin of 3.0 answered about half of the questions locally and cut the cost per question by 24.8%, 32.9% and 32.5% in three runs on 348 held-out BIRD questions (30.1% pooled) and by 19.9% on 693 KaggleDBQA and Spider-Realistic questions compared with Opus alone, at accuracy within 1.2 points of it (none of the differences significant; Figure 2, Table 2). Against Opus called directly through the API, the saving is 33.3% on 227 questions over unseen databases at equal accuracy. memorization check for LLM baselines, which we recommend other work run. Without any schema, Opus reproduces 4892% of the gold queries of BIRD train, KaggleDBQA and Spider-Realistic verbatim, so thinly prompted LLM scores on these sets partly reflect recall; with every name in the test databases changed, and on 227 new questions over databases published after its training cutoff (97.4% for Opus alone, 94.3% for the cascade), its accuracy with tool holds up (Section 6.4).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Slot filling and parallel generation. SQLNet (Xu et al., 2017) filled fixed sketch with its own prediction module per slot, after Seq2SQL (Zhong et al., 2017) had split the query into classified and decoded parts; both targeted single-table WikiSQL questions. Multi-table work moved to grammarbased decoders and intermediate representations decoded step by step (Yu et al., 2018a; Guo et al., 2019), building on sketch-then-fill decoding (Dong and Lapata, 2018). Non-autoregressive decoders (Gu et al., 2018; Ghazvininejad et al., 2019) and SmBoP (Rubin and Berant, 2021) cut the number of sequential steps, and diffusion language models (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2026) denoise iteratively, and Ma et al. (2026) evaluate them on text-to-SQL. Sketch slot filling has also been applied to multi-table Spider queries (Choi et al., 2021), and SemQL and NatSQL derive joins from the foreign-key graph (Guo et al., 2019; Gan et al., 2021b). Our closed slot grammar, with expression templates mined from training data, is filled by 7B backbone in one forward pass that returns k-best plans. Selection. Picking among candidates by execution agreement (Wang et al., 2023), trained verifier or an LLM judge is common (Ni et al., 2023; Pourreza et al., 2025). Closest to our validator, GradeSQL scores candidate queries with an outcome reward model at test time (Tritto et al., 2026); XiYan-SQL combines several generators and reorganizes their candidates for selection model (Gao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026), and MSc-SQL has small model critique several sampled queries together (Gorti et al., 2025). R3-SQL groups candidates by execution result and ranks the groups (Han et al., 2026), as MBR-exec and CodeT use execution agreement (Shi et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023); our validator instead scores each candidate on its own, and we group by result only to compute its margin and to show the agent one entry per result (more in Appendix L). Our candidates come mainly from lazy k-best enumeration over factorized decisions (Huang and Chiang, 2005); fixed-seed samples from the same slot scores fill any shortfall. Cascades and fast/slow systems. FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2024) sends query through chain of models and stops when scorer trusts the answer, AutoMix routes to larger model when smaller models self-verified answer looks wrong (Aggarwal et al., 2024), and RouteLLM trains routers on preference data to choose between strong and weak model (Ong et al., 2025); confidencebased deferral is well studied (Varshney and Baral, 2022; Jitkrittum et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024), including on answer consistency (Yue et al., 2024), like our vote-agreement baseline. For text-to-SQL, Malekpour et al. (2024) route among LLMs and argue that cascades cannot be used because weak models SQL cannot be judged before falling back; our validator margin is such judgment. ZeroNL2SQL lets small fine-tuned models write an SQL sketch that an LLM completes (Fan et al., 2024), and EllieSQL routes each question to cheaper or costlier pipeline by its estimated complexity (Zhu et al., 2025). TypeSafes Jev, System One model that returns typed decisions with probabilities instead of text and that TypeSafe describes as outputting all probabilities in parallel rather than token by token, inspired our System 1 (Almeida, 2026). SwiftSage pairs small fast model with slow LLM planner (Lin et al., 2023). Our setting differs in that the fast model is onepass slot parser whose executed, result-grouped k-best list and validator margin serve both as the routing signal and as the agents starting point. Evaluation. Execution accuracy on single database can accept wrong query that happens to match (Zhong et al., 2020); our scores share this limitation. BIRDs labels have known errors (Wretblad et al., 2024), so we report the original dev gold and label BIRDs 2025 corrected gold (BIRD Team, 2025a) separately, and we test the main differences with paired significance tests (Dror et al., 2018), clustered by database. Benchmark contamination can inflate LLM scores (Sainz et al., 2023); guided completion of benchmark instances detects it (Golchin and Surdeanu, 2024), and text-to-SQL accuracy has been shown to drop on data an LLM cannot have seen (Ranaldi et al., 2024). We apply such probes to the agent baseline itself and add renamed-schema test and post-cutoff evaluation set.

sections.title: 3 System 1: LuthorSQL
sections.content: Given natural-language question q, an external knowledge hint (evidence) e, and relational database with schema and stored contents, the text-to-SQL task is to produce an executable SQL query y. Following the BIRD benchmark 3 (Li et al., 2023b), predicted query is evaluated by execution accuracy: is correct if executing it on yields the exact same set of result rows as the ground-truth query y, written exec(y, D) = exec(y, D). Within our fast/slow architecture, System 1s role is to return an accurate candidate query from one generator pass and one validator pass on local hardware while producing score that Section 4 converts into routing confidence for System 2.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: Instead of writing SQL token by token, LuthorSQL predicts the structured query plan in single forward pass. From the predicted query plan, LuthorSQL then compiles the executable SQL code. After factorizing the plan score, LuthorSQL enumerates top-k choices of that plan, and chooses the final answer through trained validator (Figure 1). Every step is designed to alleviate different failure modes of small language models: Structured plans: Constraining output to discrete slot decisions prevents the model from generating syntax errors or hallucinating string literals. Deterministic compiler: Inferring table joins over the foreign-key graph relieves the neural network from writing complex join clauses. Factorized scoring: Scoring slots independently allows k-best candidate plans to be enumerated without autoregressive beam search. Full-query validator: Scoring the compiled SQL string allows second adapter to inspect the complete query structure and select among executed candidates.

sections.title: 3.2 Plans and Grammar Coverage
sections.content: A query plan is bounded record of discrete choices that abstracts away surface SQL syntax while capturing the semantic intent of query. Formally, each slot σ represents single structural decision over finite option set Oσ(q, D), where options correspond to schema items in S, small closed label sets, or grounded literal candidates. complete plan assigns one choice to each active slot, and our plan grammar defines the space of all valid combinations of slot choices. To ensure the model never invents filter values, filter slots can only point to finite set of literal candidates L(q, D) extracted from three sources: (1) database values matched by text span in or e; (2) numbers, dates, quoted strings, and capitalized phrases parsed directly from and e; and (3) the complete value lists of low-cardinality columns containing at most 12 distinct values. plan holds one to four projectionseach pairing schema column or row count with an aggregation operator (none, count, count distinct, sum, avg, min, or max) and an optional expression template alongside up to four filters, each specifying column, an operator, and pointer into L(q, D). Additional slots govern grouping, ordering, limits, DISTINCT, date parts, ratios, OR groups, and single level of derived tables (full slot specification and mined template counts in Appendix J). We define the coverage of as the proportion of benchmark queries with at least one plan that when compiled becomes query that returns exec(y, D). We observe 1,297/1,534 (84.6%) of the BIRD dev queries and 670/796 (84.2%) of the DECISION queries covered by converting the gold queries to plans and testing them by execution. An oracle slot model would return 1,280 (83.4%) of the dev responses. The remaining queries involve novel expression templates, ungroundable literal values, CTEs, and scalar subqueries. To address those queries we are using cascade with an unconstrained LLM agent.

sections.title: 3.3 Scoring Plans in One Forward Pass
sections.content: Our generator scores every slot in single forward pass so that the log-probability of any complete plan decomposes as sum over its individual decisions. We use OmniSQL-7B (Li et al., 2025; Hui et al., 2024) equipped with LoRA adapter as the encoder backbone. We serialize the database schema (tables, columns, types, descriptions, and sample values) as text prefix, followed by q, e, and one learned embedding token per slot σ. single forward pass over this sequence produces contextualized hidden state hσ for every slot. To represent the option set Oσ(q, D), each schema item is encoded as the mean of the hidden states across its serialized schema line, while each literal candidate in L(q, D) combines the hidden state of its mention span in q, the schema state of its host column, and an optional Values: suffix entry. Specialized lightweight heads then score the decisions: pointer heads compare hσ against schema options; choice heads apply softmax over small categorical label sets; pairwise heads pass 4 (hσ, option) pairs through small MLP to score aggregations, operators, templates, and constants conditioned on the chosen column; and value heads score literal candidates. Because these decisions factorize, the total score of plan is the sum of log-probabilities over the active decisions p: score(p) = (cid:88) dp log (d q, e, D) We train the generator with cross-entropy against execution-verified gold plans. For set-valued slots such as filters and literal candidates, where multiple target choices are simultaneously valid against negative set , we optimize multi-positive crossentropy objective in which each positive competes against all negatives without suppressing other positives: Lset = log (cid:88) iP esi esi + (cid:80) jN esj

sections.title: 3.4 From Plan to SQL
sections.content: A deterministic compiler translates each plan into executable SQL and constructs all table joins automatically, ensuring that join fails only if model hint is incorrect or the shortest relational path does not match the questions intent. Given the set of tables referenced by plans columns, the compiler connects them via minimum-cost Steiner tree over the databases foreign-key graph, guided by optional model-predicted join hints that specify required bridge tables or preferred foreign keys (declared keys cost 1, inferred keys more and hinted keys less; dead-end bridge tables are pruned). The compiler emits native SQLite syntax and transpiles queries to other enterprise SQL dialects when targeting external database engines.

sections.title: 3.5 Candidate Enumeration
sections.content: Because score(p) decomposes additively across slots, we can extract the top-k highest-scoring plans directly from the single forward pass without rerunning the backbone. best-first priority queue pops plans in increasing order of their log-probability gap from the greedy best plan, lazily expanding only the conditional decisions that plan actively uses. We discard plans that fail to compile or that compile to duplicate SQL string already in the pool, filling any remaining shortfall via fixed-seed sampling from the slot distributions. This yields up to = 32 distinct SQL queries per question, each executed read-only against with 3 timeout to form our set of executed candidates. We partition these candidates into result groups, where each group consists of all candidates that return an identical execution result table.

sections.title: 3.6 Picking an Answer with the Validator
sections.content: Because slot decisions are scored factorially, the generator cannot evaluate global interactions across complete SQL query; we therefore introduce validator, VALHARD, to inspect and score each compiled candidate in full. VALHARD is second LoRA adapter attached to the same frozen OmniSQL-7B backbone with linear scoring head. For each candidate c, it reads the serialized schema S, question q, evidence e, and compiled SQL string, outputting scalar quality score s(q, c) without access to the candidates generation rank, plan score, or execution result. We define candidate as live if it executes within the timeout and returns at least one non-NULL value. At inference time, LuthorSQL outputs the highest-scoring live candidate: ˆy = arg max live s(q, c) falling back to the highest-scoring candidate overall if no candidate is live. We train VALHARD with the generators = 32 candidate lists of BIRD-train databases. It is trained using hard negatives covering common ranking errors: near-miss wrong result groups and synthetic query perturbations (e.g., COUNT COUNT DISTINCT switching, filter removal, ORDER BY switching) kept only if they return new, wrong, non-null result on execution. Although the validator scores each candidate on its own, its training loss treats each result group as one composite option. The log-mean-exp of the result group candidates scores is used to compute the probability mass to avoid overestimating the probability mass for replicated SQL strings (Appendix D).

sections.title: 4 Pairing System 1 with an LLM Agent
sections.content: System 2 is Claude Opus 5.5 run as an agent.1 Its database tool is read-only SQLite runner, called through the shell, that can also print the schema (CREATE statements, three sample rows per table and BIRDs column descriptions); as Claude 1The agent transcripts of every held-out test and of the BIRD dev run record the model identifier claude-opus-5-5. It was run through Claude Code subagents on subscription, except the API runs of Appendix G.5; see Appendix E. 5 Code agent it also has file and shell tools, which it used to read its questions and write its answers, and it is instructed to execute at most eight queries before giving one final SQL query. Alone, this agent scores 77.26% on our 796-question selection split, against 59.05% for System 1. We combine the two in two ways. Candidate handoff. System 1 runs first. Its candidates (up to 32) are grouped by execution result and the top eight groups, ordered by validator score, go into the agents prompt as labeled options, each with its SQL, short preview of its result and how many of its candidates returned it. The agent keeps the same tool and the eight-query limit; its prompt adds the candidates and asks it to pick clearly right one without further exploration, or to write its own query only when it is confident every candidate is wrong. On 126 of the 796 questions, the ones whose gold query the grammar cannot express, System 1 was not run in our DECISION experiments, choice that uses gold; there the agent gets no candidates (under the handoff prompt) and System 1 is scored as wrong; 70 of the 400 sampled questions are of this kind. In the cascade these 126 and 26 more questions whose candidates form fewer than two result groups have no margin, so 152 questions always go to the agent. We test whether checking short list of executed answers takes fewer tool rounds than building query from the schema up. Confidence cascade. System 1 answers alone when it is confident and passes the question to the handoff setup otherwise. Confidence is the validators score margin between its top two result groups, and on DECISION the 126 out-of-grammar questions always go to the agent; the held-out tests route every question by the margin alone, with no gold. We pick the threshold with rule written down before the run: on 0.25 grid from 2.0 to 6.0, take the threshold that maximizes accuracy minus cost, valuing right answer at $1 and an agent call at its list price. Neither setup changes System 1.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Data and splits. All training data is public: BIRD train (Li et al., 2023b), Spider train (Yu et al., 2018b) and sample of SynSQL-2.5M (Li et al., 2025), each gold query kept only if its compiled plan returns the gold result (details in Appendix E). BIRD dev (1,534 questions, 11 databases) is scored with the original 2024-06-27 gold, as in most prior work, and we label rescoring against BIRDs 2025 revision (BIRD Team, 2025a) wherever it appears. From October 8 on, every design choice was made on DECISION, 796 questions from 8 BIRD-train databases that our adapters never trained on; RESERVED holds 348 more questions from the same databases. OmniSQLs own fine-tuning data includes all of BIRD train, so these databases are held out from our adapters but not from the backbone; Appendix lists the databases and other limits on how clean the splits are. We allowed at most three looks at BIRD dev from October 8: LuthorSQL used the first and the System 2 dev run the second. Metric and tests. For queries that lie outside the plan grammar G, System 1 still outputs its highestscoring valid plan when evaluated on BIRD dev, whereas on our held-out DECISION split out-ofgrammar questions are strictly scored as incorrect in all standalone System 1 arms. Latency measurements are reported on seeded 200-question DECISION sample at batch size 1 (averaging 29.6 distinct candidates per question; full hardware details in Appendix E). Paired comparisons use an exact two-sided sign-flip test over per-database summed differences, with 95% intervals by inversion; with 8 databases the smallest attainable is 2/28 0.008, so we also report question-level McNemar wins and losses. System 2 runs. Each agent run gives one Claude Code subagent 25 questions at time, with the read-only SQL tool and the prompts in Appendix K. The handoff comparison uses fixed 400-question DECISION sample with the two arms interleaved; the cascade threshold is chosen on all 796 questions after second handoff run on the other 396. Costs are Opus 5.5 list prices applied to the subagents usage logs, not invoices (Appendix E). Held-out tests. The cascade was tested on three held-out sets, each registered before any agent ran on it: RESERVED; KaggleDBQAs test split (Lee et al., 2021) and Spider-Realistic (Deng et al., 2021), on 27 databases, two of which overlap System 1s training data (Section 6.3); and new set of 227 questions over 8 databases built from public data dated after the agents training cutoff (Appendix G.3). Memorization probes, renamedschema test and attempts to raise accuracy were registered the same way (Appendices G.2 and G.4); one later exploratory search was not. Except for the API runs (Appendix G.5), the agent ran as Claude Code subagents in sandbox holding only the databases and the SQL tool, and every transcript was scanned for access outside it. sections.title: Latency
sections.content: LuthorSQL achieves competitive accuracy among fast local models while operating in under second on single GPU. On BIRD dev, the two-adapter System 1 reaches 59.39% execution accuracy (911 of 1,534 questions), placing it roughly on par with multi-sample diffusion language models with reported latency of over five seconds (a preprint result under different conditions and hardware), though behind slower autoregressive models that generate SQL token by token such as its OmniSQL-7B backbone (62.6% in our harness; Appendix F). As shown in Table 6 (Appendix F), generating only the single greedy plan takes just 0.13 end-to-end on one H100 PCIe and achieves 49.12% on DECISION. Expanding to = 32 candidates and reranking with VALHARD adds nearly ten percentage points of accuracy (+9.93 points) for roughly 0.7 of additional compute, yielding median end-toend latency of 0.84 per question ($0.64 per 1,000 queries). Zero-shot dialect transfer. Because LuthorSQL predicts an engine-agnostic query plan before compiling to SQL, it transfers across enterprise database engines without retraining. Transpiling the SQLite candidates and executing them natively on all 1,534 BIRD dev questions yields 57.159.3% on Snowflake, MySQL, DuckDB, PostgreSQL and BigQuery, compared to 60.17% in SQLite on the same database files (Table 9 in Appendix F). single local checkpoint thus serves six distinct SQL engines within 3.1-point accuracy band.

sections.title: 6.3 Pre-Registered Cascade Evaluations
sections.content: Routing queries between System 1 and the Claude Opus 5.5 agent via our pre-registered validator margin threshold (t = 3.0) answers roughly half of all questions locally and reduces API costs by 1634% with no significant loss of accuracy (Figure 2, Table 2). Across three complete runs on RESERVED (348 held-out BIRD questions), the cascade handled 49.1% of queries locally on System 1 and cut total list-price cost by 34.3% pooled against Opus with candidates (and 20.9% against Opus alone in Run 1, including rented H100 GPU cost), while matching the agents accuracy within statistical noise (0.29 points pooled against Opus with candidates, +0.96 points against Opus alone). While the first RESERVED run failed our pre-registered rule, missing its cost, time-saving and lower-bound bars (29.9% vs. 30%, 12.3% vs. 25%, and 2.60 vs. 2.50 points), the pooled runs and external benchmarks confirm that validator-margin routing consistently outperforms vote-agreement, question-length, and random routing baselines at the same call budget (Appendix G). Local hardware and direct API deployment. When System 1 runs on hardware an organization already owns, its marginal cost is purely electricity; counting local compute as zero increases the cascades cost savings against standalone Opus to 30.1% pooled on RESERVED and 19.9% on the external benchmark (Figure 2). Furthermore, quantizing the shared backbone to 8-bit weights allows both adapters to run in about 9 GB of unified memory on 24 GB Apple M3 laptop, matching GPU accuracy on 239 RESERVED questions (159 vs. 158 correct). Finally, when calling Opus directly through the plain Messages API, the = 3.0 cascade reduces API cost by 33.3% on our post-cutoff fresh benchmark at statistically indistinguishable accuracy (95.15% vs. 95.59%, = 1.0); on RESERVED, measured afterwards, it saved 35.3% but at 2.0 points lower accuracy (p = 0.03; Appendix G.5).

sections.title: Generalization
sections.content: Because frontier LLMs may have memorized public text-to-SQL benchmarks during pretraining, we ran pre-registered contamination probes before trusting our System 2 baseline. Given only question and database namewith no schema and no database toolOpus 5.5 generated executable queries that returned the gold result on 7995% of instances across four public splits and reproduced 4892% of gold SQL queries verbatim, down to dataset-specific alias conventions and backtick formatting (Table 8 in Appendix F). Standard schemaprompted evaluations on these public sets therefore mix reasoning with verbatim recall. However, two controlled robustness tests suggest that Opuss high accuracy as tool-using agent comes mostly from database exploration rather than memorization. First, when we systematically renamed every table and column in the RESERVED databases using non-Claude model and paraphrased the questions, the routed agents accuracy remained unchanged (72.88% vs. 72.32% on original schemas, = 1.0). Second, on our newly constructed benchmark of 227 verified questions over 8 databases published after the agents training cutoff (JulyOctober 2026), System 1 answered 96.1% of its kept questions correctly, the routed agent scored 92.80% against 95.2% for Opus alone on the same questions (the registered endpoint), and the full cascade achieved 94.27% accuracy against 97.36% for Opus alone (a 3.08-point gap, not significant) while cutting cost by 20.1%  (Table 2)  .

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Organizations deploying natural-language database interfaces do not have to choose between the accuracy of frontier LLM agent and the speed, privacy, and zero marginal cost of small local model. LuthorSQL, one-pass slot-filling model, reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRDs hidden test set in 0.84 on single GPU, and transfers zero-shot across six SQL engines without retraining. Placed in front of Claude Opus 5.5 as fast System 1 gate, its validator margin routes roughly half of incoming queries locally and cuts end-toend API costs by 1634% across pre-registered held-out benchmarks with no significant loss of the agents accuracy. Finally, our contamination probes show that while frontier LLMs have memorized large portions of public text-to-SQL benchmarks verbatim, tool-assisted agents maintain high accuracy on obfuscated schemas and post-cutoff databases.

sections.title: Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Limitations. The grammar expresses 84.6% of BIRD dev gold queries; questions needing CTEs, correlated subqueries, window functions or unseen templates usually go wrong, which is one reason to route them to an agent. The cascade has not yet been run on BIRDs hidden test set, and its held-out tests are small (8, 27 and 8 databases), so intervals are wide and results vary between runs; RESERVEDs first registered run failed its registered bars (Section 6.3). Time savings hold against Opus with candidates but not against Opus alone, since the routed questions are the slow ones, and agent time depends on load. Costs are list prices applied to logged usage, not invoices, and the agents ran inside Claude Code, whose fixed per-session cost makes part of the saving come from running fewer sessions; through the plain API the saving is registered on the fresh set only. Opus has probably seen every public set we used (Section 6.4); the renamed-schema test blocks verbatim recall but not recall of querys structure, and the fresh set is easier than BIRD and was checked by LLM agents and spot-checked by hand rather than reviewed in full. On BIRD dev the agent is much stronger on confident questions, so the = 3.0 threshold lost 2.93 points there; on DECISION, out-of-grammar questions were routed by gold coverage, which the held-out tests avoid. These questions were identified by converting their gold SQL, information deployed system would not have, so the DECISION cascade results assume perfect out-of-grammar detector, and in the handoff the agent saw an empty list on these questions (70 of the 400) instead of System 1s usually wrong candidates, which can mislead it; this may flatter the handoffs accuracy and change its time savings. DECISION and RESERVEDs databases are in OmniSQLs fine-tuning data. In designing VALHARD, the hard-negative perturbation categories were chosen after inspecting an earlier validators errors on DECISION, the same split used to evaluate VALHARD, so its +1.76-point gain on DECISION may be optimistic (the BIRD dev score of 59.39% played no part in its design). Furthermore, VALHARD narrowly missed our pre-written database-level significance bar on DECISION (database sign-flip = 0.19, question-level McNemar = 0.04), though we retained it as no subsequent validator modification outperformed it (Appendix B). BIRDs test score is 8.64 points above our dev score and we cannot say why without test labels; it comes from BIRDs emailed result and is not yet on the public leaderboard. Everything here is English with foreignkey joins; System 1 runs on MySQL, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, Snowflake and BigQuery through translation of its SQLite output rather than natively, the cascades agent was tested on SQLite only, and the system needs read access to the database. Future work. Next steps are the = 3.0 cascade on BIRDs hidden test set, plain-API cost measurement, native generation in other SQL dialects, caching the validators schema pass per database (about half of System 1s time), and detector that routes out-of-grammar questions before System 1 runs.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: All training and evaluation data are public; the evaluation sets are KaggleDBQA (CC BY-SA 4.0), Spider-Realistic (built from Spider dev, CC BYSA 4.0) and the fresh set, whose sources licenses are in Appendix G.3. The reported system uses BIRD (CC BY-SA 4.0), Spider (CC BYSA 4.0) and SynSQL-2.5M (Apache-2.0); earlier rounds also used WikiSQL (Zhong et al., 2017) (BSD-3-Clause), Spider-Syn (Gan et al., 2021a) (MIT), SParC and CoSQL (both CC BY-SA 4.0). OmniSQL-7B and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2024) (the model that wrote R1s rareskeleton questions) are released under Apache-2.0. The BIRD-Platinum labels of Zhu et al. (2026), for which we found no license, were used for research only: in VALHARDs training lists, which makes them part of the reported system, and in other validator and judge training and one generator experiment. No private or proprietary data was used. LLM outputs (answers from Opus 5.5, Sonnet, Haiku, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and judge verdicts) were used for evaluation, and some training questions were written by LLMs: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Claude subagents in rounds 23, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for one negative-result experiment, and Qwen2.5-14B for R1s rare skeletons. text-to-SQL system can return confident wrong answer to user who cannot read SQL; the validator margin used by the cascade is one signal for flagging such cases, not guarantee. Ibrahim Memon designed and ran the experiments and wrote the paper; Armin Karamzade gave feedback on the framing and presentation of the paper; Hanif Jhaveri advised on the work; Roy 9 Fox supervised the work. An AI assistant (Claude, through Claude Code) wrote much of the experiment code under the first authors direction and helped prepare the manuscript from the first authors notes and experiment logs; the first author revised the text and checked every number against those logs, and all authors take responsibility for the content.

sections.title: A How We Got Here
sections.content: All stages used public data only. The first version, bi-encoder on the openjev Qwen3.5-4B model (AlexWortega, 2026), encoded question and columns separately; the wrong output column caused 4861% of its errors, so later versions put the schema in front of the question. An autoregressive detour (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Hui et al., 2024; OmniSQL-32B) scored higher but cost seconds per question, so we returned to one pass on OmniSQL7B with grammar v3, which covers 1,297 of 1,534 dev gold queries (84.6%). Pooling two runs candidates gave 59.06%; the gain came from the larger candidate list, so we kept one run (R1) with up to 32 distinct plans and retrained its validator on hard negatives (VALHARD). Because no further selection change passed its bar (Appendix B) and 15% of dev questions lie outside the grammar, where model that writes SQL freely does better (35.9% against 14.8% for our system on those 237 questions), we paired System 1 with an agent instead of growing the grammar.

sections.title: B What Did Not Work
sections.content: Table 4 lists the attempts that did not survive; their scripts, costs and raw outputs are in the code release. No selection change after VALHARD passed: off-the-shelf and fine-tuned judges did not beat the trained 7B validator by the per-database test, and judge combination that gained 2.01 points on DECISION fell to +0.29 on RESERVED after we had tried about eleven configurations on the same questions, so the first number mostly measured our search. No generation change passed either: doubling the training steps, execution-reward RL, extra LLM-written rows, corrected labels and larger grammar all landed within noise or below. Two seeds of one recipe differ by 0.50 points on DECISION, which is why single-run generator claims needed +2.0.

sections.content: selection BIRD judged that two separately trained adapters belong on its Overall leaderboard and invited single-adapter resubmission for the Single Trained Model track, so we built one. It keeps R1s rank-32 adapter and slot heads and adds zero-initialized linear rerank head on the same adapters last hidden state, so no second adapter exists. Each training step combines one VALHARD validator batch with one generator chunk replayed from R1s training mix; no DECISION, RESERVED or dev question is in the training data, and inference is unchanged with one backbone in memory. Run 1 (2 epochs, generator weight 1.0) and run 2 (3 epochs, weight 0.5, chosen by rule written before run 1 was scored) are 0.75 and 0.50 points below the two-adapter system, not significantly  (Table 5)  , though the intervals are wide (run 2: [4.06, +2.74]), so this is not evidence of equal accuracy. The gap is mostly in selection: on R1s candidates both pick at 58.42% against VALHARDs 59.05%. weight average (soup) of the two runs and 2-layer rerank head did worse. We resubmitted run 2 to BIRD for its Single Trained Model track. On the hidden test set it scores 68.19% EX (simple 77.03, moderate 65.77, challenging 43.51), 69.35% Soft F1 and 64.58% RVES, against 68.03%, 69.26% and 65.17% for the two adapters, so one adapter loses no test accuracy. G.3 Fresh unseen set Eight SQLite databases were built, by Claude subagents doing data plumbing only, from public data dated 1 July 2026 or later (small reference tables excepted), each with at least three related tables and declared foreign keys: FDA enforcement reports (openFDA, CC0), USGS earthquakes and NWS alerts (US public domain), HM Land Registry price-paid data (OGL v3.0: Contains HM Land Registry data Crown copyright and database right 2021. This data is licensed under the Open Government License v3.0.), the 2026 World Cup knockout matches (openfootball, CC0), Chicago crimes and traffic crashes (City of Chicago Data Terms of Use) and Formula 1 races (Jolpica-F1, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). An MLB database was excluded because its terms forbid redistribution. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash wrote 40 questions per database with evidence and gold SQL that had to execute, be deterministic and return 1 to 1,000 rows; GLM 5.3 judged each item and the first 30 per database were kept. By an amendment recorded before any model ran, independent LLM agents (model not recorded; possibly Claude) wrote their own query before seeing the gold and judged all 240 items; 13 items with majority of wrong verdicts were removed, leaving 227, and an author checked 20 by hand and found all correct. Counting the 13 removed items as misses gives 92.1% for Opus alone and 89.2% for the cascade. The questions often name columns or codes, so they are easier than BIRDs. G.4 Raising accuracy at the same cost We registered variants of the routed agent and tested them on RESERVEDs renamed copies, split by database into development and confirmation half  (Table 14)  ; none gained the required 2 points, and the best combination, run end to end on all of RESERVED, scored 80.17% against the cascades 80.46% at saving of only 19.1%, so it was not adopted. While scoring them we found and fixed bug that had costed the baseline over all routed questions but each variant over its half, which had made the top-3 variant look 20% cheaper instead of 11%. An exploratory search with 55 agents on DECISION only ($2.98 of GPU) found no routing change worth more than 0.63 points. G.5 Opus through the API The API agent (experiments/plain_api/) calls Opus 5.5 through the Messages API with one conversation per question: the API-agent prompt of Appendix K, the schema output of the SQL tool in the user message, the read-only SQL tool with the eight-execution limit enforced in code, submit tool, at most 14 turns, default sampling, no extended thinking, and prompt caching on the system prompt and the schema, so databases schema is written to the cache once. Costs are its logged usage at the list prices of Section 5. The first registered API test on RESERVED kept the Claude Code design, in which each routed question also shows System 1s top eight candidate groups. Through the API those candidates add about 1,250 uncached input tokens and third more output per routed question ($0.0223 against $0.0122 without them) and no accuracy (86.21% against 86.49% for Opus alone), so that cascade cost 18.3% [2.3, 31.3] more than Opus alone, at 84.20% accuracy; inside Claude Code the same difference was hidden by the fixed session cost. Forwarding only the question was then registered for the fresh set before any API call there (Section 6.3). The fresh run cost $2.47 and the RESERVED run $9.62. G.6 Registration record The registrations were private files in our development repository, each hashed (SHA-256) when written, with run records and amendments appended below the registered text; every stored hash equals that of the files opening section except the external tests, whose placeholder for run details was filled in place, so its hash matches its first committed version. Table 15 gives the commit times, which are our own records rather than an external timestamp; RESERVED run 1s registration and the cross-agent predictions were first committed together with their results. Future registrations will use an external registry. Development-set use and possible leakage BIRD dev was development set in earlier rounds; after October 8, 2026 nothing was fitted or tuned on it, and LuthorSQLs configuration was hashed before its one scoring run. Some evidencerepair rules of earlier systems were written after reading dev misses; we report those systems with version rebuilt without them, and LuthorSQL does not use that repair. Two Spidertrain databases overlap dev (formula_1; soccer_1 with european_football_2); retraining without them changed DECISION accuracy by 1.01 points (p = 0.42), and on the other nine dev databases LuthorSQL scores 60.52%. OmniSQLs fine-tuning data contains all of BIRD train, so DECISION and RESERVED are held out from our adapters only. Dev gold has been public since 2023, and Opuss answers alone match its gold text on 20.9% of questions, so every agent setting was chosen on DECISION and dev agent scores are not treated as estimates for unseen questions.

Ranges give how many of each slot plan can hold. System 2 prompt and tool The routed agent received the prompt below, one per chunk of up to 25 questions, with CHUNK and OUT replaced by file paths. The agent-alone prompt, an example candidate list and the plain-API loop for the open-weight agents are in the code release. The tool is read-only SQLite runner: --schema prints the CREATE statements, three sample rows per table and BIRDs column descriptions, and query prints the column names and at most 20 rows. You are answering BIRD text-to-SQL questions (SQLite) together with fast text-to-SQL system. For each question that system already proposed candidate queries; they are grouped by identical execution result and listed best first by its own confidence (n_of_32 = how many of its 32 samples gave that result; "result" = short preview of the rows). Some questions have no candidates. Input: CHUNK (JSONL: question_id, db_id, question, evidence, candidates[{label, sql, result, n_of_32}]). Output: append one JSON line per question to OUT as soon as it is done: {"question_id": <exactly as given>, "pick": "<label>"} if one candidate answers the question correctly, or {"question_id": <exactly as given>, "pick": "NONE", "sql": "<your own SQLite query>"} if none is correct or there are none. Exactly one line per question. Tool (the ONLY thing you may use besides reading CHUNK and writing OUT): python3 TOOLS/sql.py <db_id> --schema # tables, sample rows, column descriptions python3 TOOLS/sql.py <db_id> "<SQL>" only SQL, prints up to 20 rows # runs readGet each DB's schema only if you need it, and reuse it for later questions on the same DB. Rules (strict -- this is benchmark): - Do NOT read any other file or directory (no repo files, no gold SQL, no other chunks/answers, no web). - At most 8 SQL executions per question. Use the candidates to save work: when one is clearly right, pick it without extra exploration; write your own SQL only when you are confident every candidate is wrong. - Judge correctness as the benchmark does: the result set must equal the intended answer (row order ignored). Use the evidence: it defines terms and formulas as the benchmark intends. Exactly the asked columns, nothing extra. - If you write any helper script, put it ONLY in OUT's dir + "/../work/<chunk name>/"; never create or edit shared files (other agents run in parallel). Final message: "done N/N, picked K, own M".

sections.title: L Further related work
sections.content: Autoregressive text-to-SQL. Early systems used grammar-constrained and execution-guided decoding (Scholak et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2018), alongside encoders that link question words to schema items (Wang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023a); LLM systems later added decomposition, self-correction, multi-agent pipelines and retrieval-based schema linking (Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023; Talaei et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), and benchmarks such as Spider 2.0 now pose enterprise-scale workflows for such agents (Lei et al., 2025). Several highscoring open models build on large SQL corpora: CodeS (Li et al., 2024) pretrains open models for SQL, OmniSQL (Li et al., 2025) fine-tunes 7B to 32B models on millions of synthetic examples, and Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 (Yao et al., 2026) trains with execution rewards starting from OmniSQL checkpoints. We use OmniSQL-7B as our backbone but never decode text from it. Slot filling and joins. Before multi-table benchmarks, SQLova, X-SQL and HydraNet filled WikiSQLs sketch slots from pretrained encoders (Hwang et al., 2019; He et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2020). RYANSQL is the closest multi-table precedent: it splits nested SQL into non-nested SELECT statements and fills each with sketch-based slot filling on Spider (Choi et al., 2021); our grammar is flatter (no nesting) but fills its slots from one pass of an LLM backbone and returns k-best plans. Our compilers join inference over the foreign-key graph follows natural-language interfaces that connect the tables query mentions with Steiner tree over the schema or ontology graph, as in ATHENA and Templar (Saha et al., 2016; Baik et al., 2019). Pointing at stored values rather than generating them, as our filter slots do, appears in BRIDGE and ValueNet (Lin et al., 2020; Brunner and Stockinger, 2021). Selection and verification. Contextual AIs to pick BIRD system trains reward model among generators own candidates (Agrawal and Nguyen, 2025), as VALHARD trains on hard negatives drawn from our generators candidate lists; it is described in blog post and code release, not paper. Robustness and contamination. Rajkumar et al. (2022) gave Codex questions with no database information and argued qualitatively against memorization of Spider; our schema-free probe makes the same kind of test systematic and adds verbatim matching. Dr.Spider and Spider-Syn perturb schemas and questions (Chang et al., 2023; Gan et al., 2021a), as our renamed-schema test does for the agent, and LiveSQLBench releases questions over newly built databases (BIRD Team, 2025b), the idea behind our post-cutoff set.
